rationale: The book's core equation of 'new name' with 'the renewed covenant' requires an extra definitional step (importing the chapter's specialized sense of 'know' as covenant-keeping so that the name is both known and kept only by its recipient). The printed texts themselves never identify the name with the covenant object; they treat the name as a label of transformed status or personal designation. The mainstream reading of God-given new identity/status accounts for the same verses with fewer steps, matches the actual content of the names supplied in Isaiah 62:4, matches the etymology and function of the renaming in Genesis 32:28, and fits the personal, secret token of Revelation 2:17 without redefinition. Secondary elaborations about secrecy and keeping are compatible with either view and do not rescue the core identification.
book_secondary_elaborations: known only by the one who receives it
kept only by the one who receives it (via the chapter's definition of 'know')
strongest_counter_interpretation: A 'new name' symbolizes the new identity, character, and status God confers on a redeemed person or people, marking decisive transformation of nature and relationship to God and, eschatologically, full acceptance and glorified identity.
counter_core_identification: God-given new identity, character, and status of the redeemed/overcomer
material_core_denial: The new name is not itself the renewed covenant; it is a designation of the new identity and status that the covenant confers.
counter_case: Genesis 32:28 renames Jacob 'Israel' expressly because he has 'power with God and with men, and hast prevailed,' marking a new personal status and role that becomes the identity of the covenant people.

Isaiah 62:2–5 promises a new name and immediately supplies the names Hephzibah ('my delight is in her') and Beulah ('married'), which are status descriptors of restored favor and marital covenant relationship, not the covenant itself.
Isaiah 65:15 contrasts the cursed name left to the wicked with 'another name' given to God's servants, again a mark of distinct honored status.

Revelation 2:17 presents a white stone bearing a new name known only to its recipient, a personal token of acceptance or transformed identity (consistent with ancient admission/acquittal customs and with the intimacy of individual eschatological recognition).

The broader biblical pattern of renamings (Abram/Abraham, Sarai/Sarah, Simon/Peter) uniformly signals new identity, vocation, or status under God rather than equating the name with the covenant document or relationship.
book_explanatory_advantages: Tightly links the 'no man knoweth' clause of Revelation 2:17 to the chapter's prior definition of 'know' as covenant relationship proved by obedience.
Draws on the explicit marriage and delight language of Isaiah 62:4–5 (Beulah, bridegroom rejoicing) that naturally evokes covenant renewal.
Integrates the entry with the surrounding four-office argument that love, knowing, faith, and belief all converge on covenant-keeping.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Accounts directly for the semantic content of the concrete new names supplied in Isaiah 62:4 without additional redefinition.
Explains every major biblical renaming narrative by the same mechanism (identity/status change) without special pleading.
Reads the secrecy of Revelation 2:17 as personal intimacy or unique personal designation, a reading already common and requiring no imported equation of 'know' with 'keep'.
Remains compatible with parallel Revelation texts (even if not printed here) that treat divine and civic names as marks of belonging and identity.
evidence_book_core_cannot_explain: The explicit new names of Isaiah 62:4 ('Hephzibah' and 'Beulah') function as status labels of delight and marriage, not as a designation of 'the renewed covenant' itself.
The etymological gloss in Genesis 32:28 ('for as a prince hast thou power with God…') identifies 'Israel' as a status title of prevailing power, not as the covenant.
The white stone of Revelation 2:17 is a concrete personal token containing the name, more naturally a symbol of individual identity or admission than an abstract covenant.
unresolved_objections: The book's broader method of deriving symbols uniformly from the Old Testament may still illuminate related terms ('know,' 'name,' 'sheep') even if the specific equation of new name with renewed covenant is weaker.
There is partial conceptual overlap if the new identity is understood as precisely the status enjoyed under the renewed covenant; the cores nevertheless remain distinct referents.
